_source.displaydescription:
Dune Bāhāḥ, one of the branches of Oku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260), is located in Okubāhāl Ṭola to the north of Oku Bāhāḥ. This Bāhāḥ can be accessed from two directions: either from the western side through a narrow alley between the houses opposite Mahābuddha Temple (LAL2340), or from the south through another alley passing through an open courtyard.

The monument building can be found on the west side of the courtyard and faces east. The principal façade has a main central door that is decorated with carvings of  floral details and images of the Buddhist deities. The door is flanked by two narrow openings on either side. The ground floor of the building has been plastered in cement and painted white. It is separated from the first floor by a band of carved timber cornices. A pāsukājhyaḥ with three openings can be found at the centre of the first floor with two small arched windows on either sides. Above the central window, one can find a blind window with five arched recesses; these symbolise Pañcabuddhas. This floor was recently reconstructed using local deśī apā on mud mortar (writing in 2019). The structure is covered with a sloped CGI sheet roof, and is surrounded by tall, five-storey buildings on three sides.

The courtyard contains a central Buddha shrine with three tiers (3.7m high), a Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala (50 cm high) and a Dharmadhātu Jinālaya Caitya (1.7 m high).

This Bāhāḥ was established by Punaju Śākya of Oku Bāhāḥ in NS 779 (1659 CE), which is why it is also called Pūrṇacandra Vihāra. Earlier, the god house of the monastic building had three storeys, however it was severely damaged by the 2015 earthquakes. As a result, the third floor has since been removed, and a roof of corrugated zinc sheets has been installed on top of the second floor. The façade of the first floor has a trikhājhyāla with a carved toraṇa; this is flanked by two small windows. Above the window, five niches made from terracotta symbolise the Five Buddhas. The ground floor houses the sanctum, which contains an icon of an east-facing Akṣobhya sitting in a bhūsparśa gesture. Dharmacakra Mañjuśrī sits to the left of the figure, whilst a statue of Avalokiteśvara can be found to its right. The entrance to the sanctum is flanked by two small windows but has no toraṇa. Instead, images of Akṣobhya Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā and Lokeśvara can be found above the door. A statue of a four-handed Ganeśa is housed in a niche to the right of the entrance (which lies to the south). Above this, there is a toraṇa with a further image of Gaṇeśa. Another niche to the left of the entrance (to the north) contains an image of Mahākāla; like the one on the right-hand side, this too is surmounted by a torana, this time displaying an image of Mahākāla.

_source.displaydescription:
This large bell hangs on a stone structure between two stone pillars and has a metal roof with gajuras. It was built by King Jayavishnu Malla and Queen Chandra Lakshmidevi and used for special proclamations by the Malla Kings. It is now rung during Khadgajatra in honour of the Goddess Taleju (Pruscha 1975, 162).

The Taleju Bell is located between the Hariśaṅkara Temple and Cyāsiṃ Devala in the Patan Darbar Square. Similar large bells also constructed during the Malla period can be found at Basantapur Darbar Square (Kathmandu) and the Bhaktapur Darbar Square.

This bell hangs on a stone beam supported by two stone pillars that are erected on top of a platform. To reach the platform, one must enter the inside of the plateau through a narrow door to the east of the building and climb up a ladder with 9 rungs. Above the beam, one can see a gilded copper roof, and on top of the roof there are three pinnacles topped with parasols. Small wind chimes hang down from the bottom of the roof, which in turn is supported by 16 struts. Statues of śārdūlas can be found on the struts positioned in the four corners, while other struts contain carvings of Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, Bhairava and Mātṛkās.

The body of the bell holds an inscription informing readers that it was commissioned by King Viṣṇu Malla (1729-1745) and Queen Candralakṣmī Devī. It also tells us that the work was supervised by general Mukunda Siṃha, and that this was paid for by the merchant Padma Siṃha. This inscription does not provide us any information about the intentions behind its construction. However, a Nepalese chronicle (see Bajracharya and Michaels 2016, 129) states that the King installed this bell to scare his enemies. It is said that in the Malla period, this bell was rung to let people know that a royal announcement was about to be made; upon hearing the noise, people nearby would gather near the palace. It may also have been rung to tell citizens to come together for other special occasions. There is also a legend that the bell was rung daily in the morning and evening when the palace worshipped Goddess Taleju. At present, the bell may be sounded only during special occasions in the Dashain festival (for example when the demon-dancers come to dance in Mul Chowk and sacrifice animals). Only then is the small gate to the bell's platform opened.
